title: The Orchard of Hidden Traits
markdown:
The whispers about the old Grimshaw Orchard had reached even the humming halls of Northwood High, a place usually filled with the whir of circuits and the clatter of dropped tools. Not just for its gnarled trees that twisted like ancient dancers, or the silence that clung to its perimeter as if the wind itself held its breath, but for its fruit. Fruit that played hide-and-seek with its own traits.

Ari, fingers stained with solder paste from a servo that had stubbornly jammed, stood at the orchard’s edge. Her robotics class needed a project that could marry coding to keen observation. This orchard, with fruit that reportedly skipped generations and changed identity, felt like a perfect strange challenge. Beside her, Nyx, a raven with feathers like polished obsidian, ruffled her wings. Intelligent eyes scanned the rows. Dr. Hale stood with them, a botanist whose smile was as warm as a sun-ripened peach, spectacles perched, gentle curiosity in the set of her mouth.

“They say,” Ari began, hushed, “that trees which bore star-shaped sapphire-blue plums last year are now producing perfectly round ruby-red apples. And the apples themselves? No one remembers seeing them here for decades. As if the orchard is forgetting what it used to be.”

Nyx cawed softly, a short sharp sound with weight.

Dr. Hale chuckled, warm against the quiet. “A secret language of remembering and forgetting. For a robotics project, fascinating. How do you build a system to understand something so unpredictable? How do you code for what seems to defy logic?”

Ari tapped her chin. If it were truly random, there would be no pattern. What if it wasn’t random? What if there was hidden order?

They ventured in. The air grew thick with damp soil and fallen leaves. A bee went about its business as if rumours were not its department. They stopped at a plum tree, branches stark, no legendary sapphire fruit.

“Last year, this one,” Dr. Hale pointed, “produced the most beautiful star-shaped plums. Deep blue, almost indigo. Taste like moonlight and honey, they said.” She said it without theatre. The tree, being a tree, did not comment.

Nyx hopped onto a low branch, peered at the soil, nudged a fallen leaf, and pointed with a deliberate beak at a small round object half-buried: a tiny bright red apple, looking frankly embarrassed to be a clue.

Ari knelt, knees in the soft earth. A plum tree. Why apples? The incongruity sent a shiver. A small gasp escaped.

“Precisely,” Dr. Hale said, eyes twinkling. “And not just this tree.” She gestured to a towering apple tree laden with gleaming ruby fruit. “Perfectly round. Skin so smooth. Yet at the base of the trunk—” a cluster of star-shaped sapphire plums nested among exposed roots, a vibrant splash of the wrong colour in the right place.

Nyx clicked, head cocked, then flew to a different plum tree bearing ordinary lumpy green fruit. She pecked, drawing Ari’s gaze to a small withered bud on a higher branch. Ari squinted. The bud was not the familiar green of a plum bud. It was a faint ethereal blue, and when she brushed away dust she saw the delicate outline of a star forming within it.

“Wait,” Ari said, energy arriving all at once. “Nyx, you’re onto something. What if the traits don’t disappear? What if they wait their turn? What if the plum tree isn’t actually growing apples, but its plum trait is dormant this year, and an apple trait from some distant ancestor is showing? And the apple tree is doing the opposite — ancient plum heritage making an appearance.”

Dr. Hale’s smile broadened, slow and knowing. “Inheritance. Not in people or animals, but in plants. Characteristics passed from parents to offspring. Sometimes a trait is expressed strongly, like a loud voice. Sometimes it’s hidden, a whispered secret, only to reappear later — a grandchild, a great-grandchild.”

Ari’s mind raced, connections compiling, the orchard suddenly as readable as a stubborn circuit. “So a plum tree can produce apple-like fruit, or an apple tree plum-like fruit, if there’s a hidden plum gene in the apple ancestry and a hidden apple gene in the plum’s, passed down. Traits might skip a generation, or two, before they show.” She pointed at the odd green plums and the budding star. “That bud isn’t a typical green plum bud. It’s a tiny immature version of last year’s star-shaped sapphires. And the apples — their roundness is so exaggerated, as if they’re emphasising their apple-ness.”

Dr. Hale nodded. She did not turn the rows into a lecture hall. She named the thing once, like labelling a well-made tool. “Genetics. Traits passed down, sometimes hidden, sometimes expressed. A complex, beautiful, logical system of inheritance.”

“A biological code,” Ari whispered. “It determines what you’ll be, and what you might become, even if you don’t see it right away. We can code for that. A program to track patterns, to predict what fruit might appear next season from the hidden traits. Not magic. Memory, written in living things.”

Nyx gave a satisfied clatter and began to preen, work done, as if genetics had been her idea and she was being modest about it.

The orchard was no longer only strange. It was a living laboratory, hidden narratives in every seed. Ari looked at her notebook, then at the trees that had seemed ordinary five minutes ago and now looked like archives. She could not wait to start coding. What other secrets were hiding in plain sight?
characters: Ari (a robotics student), Nyx (an obsidian-feathered raven), Dr. Hale (a peach-warm botanist)
